https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Green Power List 2021: the UK’s top 20 environmentalists
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Joss Garman was one of the first to be arrested. Before dawn on a Monday in October 2007, the 22-year-old and 50 other environmental campaigners invaded Kingsnorth power station in Kent. Eon, which owned and operated the station, had applied for planning permission to build a coal-burning facility on the site — the first of a wave of new power stations planned for the country.
The strategy for the protest was simple: flood the site with so many activists that the security team could not halt them all, and shut down the station. “We stayed in a farmhouse in bunks the night before, got up at 3am and all got into minibuses,” Garman, now 35, recalls. “We climbed the fence and went through these dusty tunnels.”
Garman chained himself to a conveyor belt to prevent coal from reaching the furnaces. “I was there about eight hours before I was arrested.” He was convicted of aggravated trespass and fined several hundred pounds.
It was no shock to him. A veteran of direct action, by then he had already been arrested more than 20 times. As a co-founder of the campaign group Plane Stupid, Garman had seen the door of his student house kicked down following a protest at an airport. The police accused him of terrorism. Nearly a decade and a half later he lives a very different life. The UK director of the influential European Climate Foundation, he has worked in parliament, directed think tanks and has established strong links within government and to MPs across the political spectrum. He is, in short, a key member of the environmental establishment.
● Joss Garman● Chris Packham● Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah● Sir David Attenborough● Isabella Tree● Alok Sharma● Gail Bradbrook● Carrie Johnson● Craig Bennett● Joan Edwards● Tony Juniper● Dr Emily Shuckburgh● Emma Pinchbeck● Professor Ed Hawkins● Lord Goldsmith of Richmond Park● Baroness Worthington● Angus Lunn● Chris Stark● Caroline Lucas● Derek Gow
His story is not uncommon. The following list of influential environmentalists, climate scientists and politicians includes several former activists who now occupy influential roles in and around government. Tony Juniper, a former director of Friends of the Earth and a veteran of the 1990s Newbury Bypass protests, is now chair of Natural England. Bryony Worthington, also previously of Friends of the Earth, now sits in the House of Lords and runs an environmental charity with a £70 million annual budget. Craig Bennett, yet another Friends of the Earth alumnus, is the current CEO of the Wildlife Trusts.
So has the green movement finally grown up? Garman believes the goals have shifted fundamentally. “The nature of the challenge is different today,” he says. The year after the Kingsnorth protest government plans for a new fleet of coal-powered fire stations were quietly shelved. By 2020 only 1.6 per cent of British electricity came from coal, compared with more than a third in 2007. “We have the greenest electricity in the world,” Garman says. “We’ve made huge progress and we have the carbon targets in place. The real nature of the challenge now is: how do you actually deliver?”
Emma Pinchbeck, 34, also emerged from the environmental movement. A former campaigner at WWF-UK, she was appointed last year to be CEO of Energy UK, becoming the face of the industry Garman was making trouble for all those years ago.
“The thing that I loved most about being in an NGO was that your only job is to tell the truth,” Pinchbeck says. “I miss the purity of that but I love my job now, the combination of the moral mission with the practical delivery, the pragmatism. I can see change happening every single day.
“The really big challenges in the next decade will be around technology progress, which involves quite boring government policy work. But that’s why I choose to do what I do, because I can see that’s where we need to do the most acceleration.”
For Pinchbeck, her upbringing in the Gloucestershire town of Stroud was instrumental to her environmentalism. “It’s a mix of traditional small-c conservatism with a mad, creative alternative art scene,” she says. “When I was growing up there were always protests on the high street, against the backdrop of this really pretty English town.”
That same town in 2018 witnessed the formation of Extinction Rebellion, a protest movement that burst into being in the front room of Gail Bradbrook’s council house in Stroud. Bradbrook, 49, insists direct action is still needed. She was arrested just last month on suspicion of conspiracy to cause criminal damage and fraud linked to her group’s attacks on banks and other financial institutions.
“We stand on the shoulders of those trying to get action for many, many years,” she says. “But what we need right now is to go into emergency mode. We have to go all out to get change.”
Wildlife presenter and conservationistBest known for TV shows such as the BBC’s Springwatch and The Really Wild Show, Packham has introduced entire generations to conservation and wildlife. But in recent years he has become more politically active, co-founding in 2019 the campaign group Wild Justice. The organisation saw immediate success, mounting a challenge to the right of landowners to shoot 16 bird species seen as pests — including crows, magpies and wood pigeons. Natural England acknowledged the group’s argument and withdrew the licences with 36 hours’ notice, triggering fury across rural communities.
Packham, who has also fiercely criticised badger culling, has been targeted as a result, with dead crows, a fox and a badger left in front of his New Forest home during the past two years. “We can’t have a letterbox in our door any more,” he says, because excrement was repeatedly pushed through. Nevertheless he is determined to keep campaigning. “The reason I’m increasingly vocal is that I’m now 60 years old,” he says. “I’m running out of time, and I’ve got this burden on my shoulders. We’ve lost 68 per cent of the world’s wildlife, the human population has shot up to seven-point-something billion and the world has warmed up by a degree. And that’s all been on my watch.”
Clean air campaignerIn December the coroner Phillip Barlow found that the death in 2013 of nine-year-old Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah was contributed to by her exposure to “excessive air pollution”. The verdict — the first time air pollution had been listed as a cause of death in the UK — was the result of a long campaign by her mother, Rosamund. Ella lived 25 metres from South Circular Road in Lewisham, southeast London, where air pollution levels regularly exceeded the annual legal limit. Rosamund, who set up the Ella Roberta Family Foundation after her daughter’s death, says: “The first aim was to find out how Ella died. But it was also to make sure no child goes through what she went through.” In April the coroner published a report calling for national pollution limits to be reduced in light of Ella’s death.
BroadcasterAbout 20 different species — including a spider, a butterfly and a dinosaur — are named after Attenborough, as well as an entire constellation. As the 95-year-old explained in a 2017 interview: “It’s easy to be a national treasure if you don’t have to do controversial things.” That, however, is to undersell his influence. His overwhelming contribution to environmentalism has been to inspire a love of nature — he has made more than 100 documentaries stretching across seven decades. But in recent years these have done more than simply entertain. His Blue Planet II series, broadcast in 2017, triggered a consumer backlash against plastic packaging and his recent programmes have focused heavily on climate change. In November he will address the Cop26 UN climate conference in Glasgow, in his government-appointed role as “people’s advocate” to the summit. Addressing the UN Security Council in February at the invitation of Boris Johnson, he described Cop26 as possibly “our last opportunity to make the necessary step change” towards protecting the planet.
Author and conservationist Tree is the author of the rewilder’s handbook Wilding, which chronicles the 20-year transformation of the 3,500-acre Knepp Castle estate in West Sussex, which Tree and her husband have turned over to nature. She is currently one of the most influential environmental thinkers in Britain. This was highlighted last month when the environment secretary, George Eustice, referred to her ideas in a speech on the future of the English landscape, to the delight of his audience.
Rewilding’s advocates tout it as a solution to many of our problems: it promises flood mitigation, biodiversity improvement, carbon sequestration and a balm for our battered mental health. Tree, 56, has hosted politicians at Knepp and was recently invited to discuss the government’s action plan for trees with Defra officials. While the concept of rewilding is fashionable among environmentalists, many farmers oppose it. But Tree says: “Rewilding shouldn’t be seen as the enemy of farming. If anything it is its greatest ally. It can restore soils, reduce flooding, clean water, support pollinating insects and reduce the need for pesticides. The way forward is a meshing between rewilding and regenerative agriculture.”
President of Cop26If the Cop26 UN climate summit, due to take place in Glasgow in November, is to be a success, much depends on Sharma. The 53-year-old, who will preside over the conference, has the task of getting the US, China, India and the powerful negotiating blocs of the developing world to agree to play ball. To this end he has spent the past few months flying around the globe on a diplomatic crusade. He has already found a strong ally in John Kerry, Joe Biden’s climate envoy. Last month’s meeting of G7 environment ministers, which Sharma hosted, secured a crucial agreement to stop funding overseas coal. He says: “Cop26 is our last hope of limiting global warming to 1.5C and building a brighter future of green jobs and cleaner air. The single most powerful thing we can do to get there? Consign coal to history.”
Co-founder of Extinction RebellionA mother of two with a PhD in molecular biophysics, Bradbrook co-founded the Extinction Rebellion protest movement three years ago. The inspiration for her movement? A session on hallucinogenic drugs while in Costa Rica in 2016. She described the effects in a video posted online in 2019: “This voice said ‘resistance’. I’ve never been the same since.” XR, as her organisation is known, thrust itself into the spotlight in the spring of 2018, blocking bridges and causing havoc across London. While many question the group’s tactics, there is no doubt it contributed to driving climate change up the political agenda. A few months later Theresa May committed the UK to net zero carbon emissions by 2050, the first G7 country to do so. “We said we wanted net zero by 2025, but the government has set an interim target of 78 per cent by 2035, ” Bradbrook says. “To some extent our demands have been met, but not fully. But we’ve shifted the window.”
Communications director of the Aspinall Foundation The prime minister’s wife is widely regarded as the key to his new-found environmentalism. Carrie, 33, who first met Boris Johnson during his 2012 London mayoral campaign, is a passionate conservationist and a patron of the Conservative Animal Welfare Foundation. She also works for the Aspinall Foundation, which runs two wildlife parks in Kent. Carrie is also thought to have influenced the decision to phase out the UK badger cull — to the extent that the National Farmers’ Union mounted a judicial review when a planned cull in Derbyshire was cancelled, claiming Carrie had influenced the “irrational” decision. The High Court rejected the case, ruling that there was “nothing irrational” about what had been a “political judgment”.
CEO of the Wildlife TrustsLast autumn Bennett came up with a new concept for conservation. More than 80 years after “green belts” were first implemented as a way to control expanding cities, he proposed a new “wild belt” designation to protect Britain’s nature. Green belts predominantly are made up of intensively farmed agricultural land, sprayed with pesticides and home to very little wildlife. “[They are] not actually very green,” Bennett says. Wild belts, however, would be reserved for nature and prioritise biodiversity. The idea has quickly caught on. The prime minister, speaking at the Conservative Party conference in October, said his vision of a future Britain included people “going for picnics in the new wild belts”. Bennett, 49, admits he was surprised: “When we launched it last year it was just a sketch of an idea. And within a month Boris Johnson was quoting it in his speech.”
It is a mark of the influence of Bennett and the organisation he joined last April. At his previous employer, Friends of the Earth, with whom he spent 20 years on and off including five as CEO, he developed a reputation as a “modern eco-general” — mobilising opposition to fracking during the David Cameron years. But the Wildlife Trusts is far more influential in the UK, with more than 870,000 members to Friends of the Earth’s 100,000. It also has a deeper reach into middle England, a collective turnover of £157 million and owns 2,600 nature reserves. Bennett spends much of his time visiting farms with the goal of buying them up and turning them into rewilded havens.
Director of marine conservation at the Wildlife TrustsA marine scientist for 30 years, Joan Edwards, 57, has spent her career mobilising support for legal protections for the sea. She led a coalition of environmental organisations that pushed through the Marine and Coastal Access Act in 2009, paving the way for a “blue belt” of marine conservation zones established around the coast. But Edwards thinks we need to go further, and wants 30 per cent of the world’s oceans to be covered by “highly protected marine areas” where fishing, drilling of the seabeds, even offshore wind turbines are banned. “We think that’s essential because we don’t even know what a recovering marine environment looks like,” she says.
Chair of Natural EnglandA world-renowned environmentalist, Juniper, 60, has spent his career working for campaign groups such as Friends of the Earth and WWF-UK but now the poacher has turned gamekeeper. In 2019 he was appointed chair of the government agency Natural England. He promised to build bridges with farmers’ groups after they raised doubts about his appointment. Despite his radical past, his ability to network has never been in doubt — he has served as special adviser on sustainability to the Prince of Wales.
Climate scientist at the University of CambridgeA mathematician and climate scientist, Shuckburgh, 47, is one of the country’s best communicators of the science of climate change. She is co-author — with the Prince of Wales and Tony Juniper — of the Ladybird book Climate Change. The brainchild of Prince Charles, the book provides a simple guide to an incredibly complex subject and sets out ideas that will soon affect everyone’s lives. Shuckburgh is currently most focused on her role as the director of Cambridge Zero, the University of Cambridge’s climate change initiative, which is drawing up blueprints for a zero-carbon future. A former government adviser, she also leads a national programme investigating artificial intelligence and its applications for predicting environmental risk.
CEO of Energy UKLast July Pinchbeck was headhunted to be the face of the British energy industry. Coming from Renewable UK, the trade body for the wind and solar industry, and as the former head of climate change and energy at WWF-UK, she was a perfect fit for the sector’s commitment to decarbonisation. But Pinchbeck, 34, admits she had initial concerns that she was being hired for PR purposes. “We had a long conversation about it at my interview,” she says. “From my side, it was about how much I could use my experience to help the industry transform. I took the job because I was content it wasn’t greenwashing. That has continued to be the case.”
It has not all been plain sailing. “The energy sector is fully on board with decarbonisation,” she says. “But there are differences of opinion about how we get there.” So far, however, the industry can be proud of its record. Cheap wind and solar power has caused fossil fuel use to plummet in recent years. “It’s been a fantastic success story in the UK,” says Pinchbeck, who has a 20-month-old daughter. “She’ll be almost the age I am now in 2050, by which time we will have to have decarbonised the global economy. I think about that all the time. I am deadly serious about this.”
UK director of the European Climate FoundationWhile at university Garman co-founded the campaign group Plane Stupid, which opposed the third runway at Heathrow. He co-ordinated several high-profile protests, including draping a huge banner from the roof of the Houses of Parliament. By the time he graduated he had been arrested more than 20 times. Some 14 years later he runs the UK branch of one of the most influential philanthropic environmental organisations in the world: the European Climate Foundation funds think tanks such as the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, online publications such as Carbon Brief and political bodies such as the Conservative Environment Network. Now in charge of a budget worth millions of pounds, the 35-year-old is a key player in the environmental establishment, with strong links to the government’s Cop26 unit, MPs across the political spectrum and journalists across Fleet Street.
Minister of state for Pacific and the EnvironmentZac Goldsmith, 46, is considered to be a key driver of the more radical green policies in government. His younger brother Ben, 40, also plays a key role in the Conservative Environment Network. Lord Goldsmith says: “The single most important thing governments, individuals, businesses and civil society can and must do is to throw ourselves into protecting ecosystems on land and sea, and restoring those that have been degraded. The magic of helping nature recover — beyond saving beautiful species — is that in doing so we’re tackling so many other problems we face: climate change, hunger, poverty, pollution, even pandemics.”
Co-director of the Quadrature Climate FoundationMore than anyone else, Bryony Worthington is considered to have been the driving force behind the 2008 Climate Change Act. The legislation for the first time made emissions cuts legally binding, compelling successive governments to take action on global warming. First as an activist at Friends of the Earth, then as a civil servant, Worthington built support for and then helped draft the necessary legislation. The key, she says, was creating a “legal metronome” that set five-yearly carbon budgets. “They don’t stop coming, no matter which government is in power.” Worthington, 49, was made a Labour peer in 2011 and served on Ed Miliband’s front bench before leaving the party in 2017, when Jeremy Corbyn was in charge, to become a crossbencher. She now runs the Quadrature Climate Foundation, one of the biggest philanthropic climate organisations, which has an annual budget of £70 million.
Northumbrian conservationistDescribed by friends as the archetypal “boots-on-the-ground” nature conservationist, Lunn, 87, is credited with the restoration of an entire ecosystem in Northumberland. The retired university lecturer spent decades battling the Forestry Commission over the planting of Kielder Forest, the largest manmade woodland in England. “Until the 1980s it was a completely philistine organisation,” he says. “They were hellbent on planting conifers on every bit of land they could get their hands on.” He produced the first detailed vegetation map of the area in the 1950s, identifying the Border Mires network of peat bogs in and around Kielder, the first step in the process of saving them from the foresters. His organisation, the Northumberland Wildlife Trust, then leased pockets of land from the commission in order to ensure their survival.
CEO of the Climate Change CommitteeThe Climate Change Committee, overseen by Chris Stark, devises the five-year carbon budgets that determine the pace of Britain’s decarbonisation. Stark, 42, was appointed in 2018, with the government committing to the legally binding Net Zero target the following year. Stark also drew up the interim target of cutting emissions by 78 per cent by 2035, which was adopted by Boris Johnson in April. A strong communicator, Stark is highly respected by the government. One source said he is “the number-cruncher in chief, a calming voice of reassurance to ministers grappling with what to do next”. Stark says: “We have a lot to do in the UK, changes to transport, changes in the home, new industries, new jobs, but these will be positive overall for our way of life. And the move to zero carbon is permanent, so let’s celebrate being the generation that will get the job done.”
Green Party MP for Brighton PavilionIn 2010 Caroline Lucas became the first Green to be elected to parliament. More than a decade on she has been re-elected three times, increasing her share of the vote each time. She remains the sole Green in the Commons, but the party, which she has twice served as leader, is on the rise. The local elections last month saw a record result for the party, increasing its number of council seats by 99 to 155 and making gains in regions of the UK that have never elected Greens before. Lucas, 60, has earned the respect of MPs across the party benches. She is a vocal member of the Commons Environmental Audit Committee. Asked what would be the single most important action the government could take on climate change, she says: “Redesign the economy to make meeting people’s needs within the Earth’s finite natural limits the Treasury’s No 1 goal, rather than the destructiveness of infinite economic growth.”
Guerilla rewilder A decade ago beavers escaped from Gow’s nature reserve on the Devon-Cornwall border. “A badger dug into one of our central holding pens and a bunch of beavers got out,” he says. They have spread along the River Tamar, where several generations now live in complete freedom. Natural England reported Gow, 56, to the police, but the officers decided to take no action. “They decided it was an act of God,” he says. “Because we did not knowingly let them out, that was that.”
A time is approaching when the police would not even be involved. Gow, formerly a conventional farmer whose land is increasingly given over to breeding and nurturing endangered species such as wildcats, water voles and white storks, is a hero to the rewilding movement. And his ideas are gradually becoming mainstream. The environment secretary, George Eustice, last month announced the creation of a “species reintroduction taskforce”, which will explore the prospect of bringing back a raft of animals including golden eagles, wildcats and pine martens to parts of England, as well as further beaver releases. Gow says it is about time. “What beavers do is repair the terrible damage we have done. They are the healers of the Earth’s crust. But do we need another consultation? Learning is good, but learning at the expense of actually doing is fatal.”
Professor Ed HawkinsClimate scientist at Reading University
In the summer of 2016 Hawkins was watching the opening ceremony of the Rio Olympics when he recognised a familiar dancing shape on the screen. “They had a little segment about climate change and up popped my spiral graphic, being sent out to about a billion people,” he says. The graphic, which expands in a circular motion, illustrates the way global temperatures have risen over time. Another of Hawkins’s images, which uses coloured stripes to represent the same trend, has appeared on magazine covers and the stage of concerts and festivals. “We need to reach people who don’t normally engage with science,” says Hawkins, 44. “And so we needed a very simple visual way to communicate the key message that the world is warming.” Aside from his communications work, Hawkins is highly respected as a climate scientist. He is a lead author on a key Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report due to be published in August, which will provide world leaders with the latest assessment of how quickly the world is warming.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/.title: Joe Biden arrives in UK for G7 summit
https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/.text:
Joe Biden has landed in the UK for the G7 summit in Cornwall, his first overseas visit since becoming US president in January.
The president and his wife, Jill, touched down in Air Force One at RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk this evening.
He was expected to address a crowd of US air force personnel there before flying on to Cornwall for the summit, which begins in Carbis Bay on Friday.
Hundreds of British troops, including bomb disposal teams and a navy warship, are joining more than 5,000 police officers and a 400-strong US Secret Service team at the summit this weekend in one of the biggest security operations undertaken in Britain.
The armed forces are being drafted in to help police as world leaders, their entourages and thousands of protesters descend for the three-day summit.
In the most visible show of strength, HMS Northumberland, a Type 23 frigate, will be positioned off the coast and use its radar system to help police identify potential threats from the air and sea. Military sources said plans were under discussion to deploy HMS Prince of Wales, a Queen Elizabeth-class aircraft carrier undergoing trials, in a second show of muscle.
There will also be two offshore patrol vessels, six Archer class P2000 patrol vessels and a number of rigid inflatable boats to help with surveillance.
The military has already deployed a Giraffe agile multibeam radar system that can identify and track aircraft, helicopters and ballistic targets while providing coastal surveillance.
Several explosives ordnance disposal teams and 15 explosives search dogs and handlers from the army will also operate under police command.
Armed police officers will patrol nearby waters in case they need to stop suspicious vessels as well as along the routes that VIPs will take between the airport, the summit venue at Carbis Bay Hotel, and Tregenna Castle Resort, the 98-bedroom hotel where leaders are staying.
Police will not say how many armed officers are being deployed in total but all will be armed with Heckler & Koch carbines that can fire 750 rounds a minute and are equipped with Kevlar body armour.
The airspace above Cornwall is largely shut but police are reserving the option to deploy one of their 18 drones if necessary. Last month the force said it had planned for every eventuality on land, sea and air.
MS Silja Europa, a cruise ship, has docked at Falmouth where it is preparing to accommodate 1,000 of the police officers deployed from elsewhere.
President Biden, who arrives in Cornwall tonight, will be guarded by a team housed in 50 luxury recreational vehicles around the hotel grounds.
Air Force One will land at RAF Mildenhall and Biden will leave by helicopter for the castle.
On Monday two Sea King and three Osprey helicopters could be seen scouting the route he will take. They were flown from the US in a Boeing C-17 Globemaster III with two of the armoured Cadillacs used as the presidential limousine, nicknamed the Beast.
The 18ft “White House on wheels” has ballistic armour and a sealed cabin with independent oxygen support capable of withstanding a nuclear, biological or chemical attack. Its doors are 8in thick. The cabin carries at least two pints of the president’s blood for use in an emergency transfusion.
Chevrolet Suburbans with police lights will carry the president’s Secret Service detail. One, the Halfback, follows the Beast and its decoy and carries the president’s security detail, his first line of back-up. The convoy also transports a counter-assault team of heavily armed commandos.
Another vehicle, the Watchtower, is an electronic countermeasures vehicle that jams communications and remote detonating devices to protect from explosive attack.
One, the Halfback, follows the Beast and its decoy and carries the president’s security detail, his first line of back-up. The rear-facing third row seating carries an agent with an automatic assault rifle pointing from the window. Several more Chevrolets with police lights carry the Secret Service’s counterassault team (CAT) of heavily armed elite commandos.
The CAT has the task of responding if the convoy comes under attack or forming a defensive buffer while the president’s security detail works to evacuate him from the scene. A black truck works as a hazard material mitigation unit, carrying gear to detect and respond to nuclear, biological or chemical threats.
Of the five helicopters, one becomes Marine One when the president is on board while a second accompanies it everywhere it flies as a decoy.
The cost of policing the summit has been put at £70 million although the use of mutual aid officers means that Devon and Cornwall police do not bear the cost alone.
Environmental and anti-capitalist protesters have vowed to disrupt proceedings, prompting police to shut down all bridges over the A30, the main road running through Cornwall, for up to three weeks.
Residents living behind the towering metal fences erected around the site are only permitted entry with two forms of identification.
Extinction Rebellion has said it expects about 1,000 protesters to make their way to St Ives, next to Carbis Bay, for the summit. “We have done our best to plan our actions to be peaceful, creative, artistic and Covid-safe,” the group wrote in an open letter to locals last week. “We sincerely apologise in advance for any additional disruption that we cause.”

image.caption: HMS Tyne just off the coast at the G7 summit site in St Ives, Cornwall
The coast around the G7 summit is also being patrolled by police
A mobile radar station has been set up at a National Trust car park in Godrevy, near St Ives
A USAF Osprey helicopter at RNAS Culdrose. The airspace above Cornwall is largely closed but police may use drones
Members of a Christian group start a four-day pilgrimage on foot to Carbis Bay to protest against climate change
The president and first lady arrived in Britain on Air Force One this evening

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Staying safe as a photographer at an antivax clash
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
I had just finished a morning assignment and was sitting in my car in Westminster listening to the radio and watching the rain hit my windscreen. I could hear sirens and a police van rushed passed me heading towards Parliament Square. That’s not a big deal in this part of town, but things changed when a second and third van raced past with sirens blaring. So I left my car and gathered my cameras.
It was an anti-lockdown and antivax protest on June 21, the date that was once known as “freedom day”.
It’s important as a news photographer, when covering events like this, to be seen to be impartial. I wanted police and protesters alike to see that I was not part of the demonstration but a member of the working media.
There have been times in the past when I have been turned on by the protestors and sought protection behind police lines and the police have not let me through, thinking I’m a part of the demonstration I was trying to get away from.
As I watched the protestors I saw another photographer I know from a big news agency. He felt the same as I did; that the situation was tense. The demonstration, heavily hemmed in by the police, still managed a lap of Parliament Square but then turned back up Whitehall stopping outside the gates of No 10 and blocking both roads of traffic.
I saw a wall of police standing passively as all manner of personal insults were yelled at them. I’ve seen this type of personal verbal abuse directed at the police by all sides from far-right demonstrations, Brexit protests and Extinction Rebellion demonstrations.
The police started to move the demonstrators away from Whitehall and were pushing those who deliberately stopped in their path provoking howls of anger from others.
The vitriol was getting worse when suddenly some police officers broke from the main line and made an arrest. As they tried to pull the man back to the line the man thrashed violently causing the two officers to lose their balance and fall. A small but loud crowd who saw the officers fall surged towards them.
Within seconds the main line drew their batons and pushed and beat the crowd back away from the officers still struggling with their arrest on the ground, forming a guard around them.
When sudden moments of action like that happen I just keep the camera to my eye and keep shooting. What happened was so fast that I had no idea what was in focus and what wasn’t. I could see the line of police with their batons out and one of them swing at a protester who tried grabbing the back of an officer.
A police officer suddenly moved in front of me, obscuring my view. I still had the camera to my face as I stepped back but carried on photographing. She turned to me and angrily pointed and shouted at me to “get back!” I immediately did as instructed. (I’m here to get pictures not be part of the problem.)
It’s a peculiar thing when photographing quick action that it’s only when I get the laptop open that I can see what it was I was actually photographing. I was aware that I had caught some of the action when the police moved in to protect the arresting officers but did I manage to capture that police officer running in with his baton raised? How in focus was the moment the police rushed forward? A lot of it was just a blurred jumble of fluorescent yellow jackets and unusable. But I had something dramatic and that, as a photographer, is all that matters.
The pictures were taken using a Canon EOS 5D mkIV digital SLR camera with a 24-70mm f2.8 lens at 1/500th sec, f3.2 using auto ISO

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Amazon destroys lorry-loads of unsold TVs and computers
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
Amazon is destroying millions of unsold items every year in the UK including smart TVs, laptops and top of the range headphones, an investigation suggests.
An Amazon worker secretly filmed evidence of the waste over several months at the warehouse where he worked and passed the video to ITV News. It shows items that were unsold or returned by customers being sorted into boxes marked “destroy” at Amazon’s warehouse in Dunfermline, Fife.
Documents inside the warehouse show that in one week in April more than 124,000 items were marked to be destroyed. By contrast, only 28,000 items were marked “donate” in the same seven-day period.
The worker, who has now left Amazon, said: “From a Friday to a Friday, our target was to generally destroy 130,000 items a week. I used to gasp. There’s no rhyme or reason to what gets destroyed. Dyson fans or Hoovers, the occasional MacBook and iPad. The other day, 20,000 Covid masks still in their wrappers.
“Overall, 50 per cent of all items are unopened and still in their shrink wrap. The other half are returns and in good condition. Staff have just become numb to what they are being asked to do.”
ITV News said it had tracked lorries carrying goods from the warehouse to a recycling centre and landfill site.
Amazon said it did not send anything to landfill in the UK and that the landfill site visited by a lorry was also a recycling centre.
ITV News said that Amazon’s business model resulted in huge volumes of stock being destroyed. This is because many vendors pay Amazon to house their products in its warehouses and if they are not sold it can be cheaper to get rid of them.
Sam Chetan-Welsh, political adviser to Greenpeace UK, said: “Expensive products that took energy and resources to manufacture come straight off the production line and into our overstretched waste system, and the high taxes needed to dispose of it all aren’t being paid by Amazon.”
Philip Dunne, Conservative chairman of the Commons environmental audit committee, added: “How can Amazon protest its sustainability credentials with a straight face?”
Amazon has faced similar accusations of destroying unsold stock in France and Germany. New laws in both countries make it more difficult for retailers to destroy new goods.
An Amazon spokesman said: “We are working towards a goal of zero product disposal and our priority is to resell, donate to charitable organisations or recycle any unsold products. No items are sent to landfill in the UK.
“As a last resort, we will send items to energy recovery [in which goods are put in incinerators that generate electricity], but we’re working hard to drive the number of times this happens down to zero.” The spokesman declined to give a breakdown of the number or proportion of items that were donated, recycled or incinerated.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.title: Euro 2020: Fans injured by Greenpeace parachute protester
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.text:
Uefa has confirmed that “several people” are being treated in the hospital for injuries caused by a Greenpeace protester who parachuted into a football stadium before France’s victory over Germany in their Euro 2020 game in Munich.
European football’s governing body said that the “law authorities will take the necessary action” for what it called a “reckless and dangerous” act.
Debris fell onto the pitch and into the stands when the parachutist got tangled in wires carrying an overhead camera. France’s head coach, Didier Deschamps, was seen having to duck out of the way of a large piece of equipment that fell near the dugout.
The activist, who was protesting against Volkswagen, the tournament sponsor, had the words “Kick out oil! Greenpeace” written on his parachute. He landed heavily on the pitch and was given medical attention before being escorted away by security.
A statement from Uefa said: “This inconsiderate act ... caused injuries to several people attending the game who are now in hospital and law authorities will take the necessary action.
“Uefa and its partners are fully committed to a sustainable Euro 2020 tournament and many initiatives have been implemented to offset carbon emissions. The staging of the match was fortunately not impacted by such a reckless and dangerous action, but several people were injured nonetheless.”
Greenpeace’s German Twitter account confirmed that the stunt was a protest against Volkswagen, and demanded an end to the sale of petrol and diesel cars.
When the match eventually got under way it was won 1-0 by France after a Mats Hummels own goal in the first half.

image.caption: As he descended, the parachutist was caught on cables carrying an overhead camera
Debris dislodged by the impact rained down on fans as well as on Didier Deschamps, the French coach
